sections.title: Omakase Sushi
sections.desc: Tokyo holds more Michelin stars than any city on earth — and nowhere is this more felt than at its sushi counters. Expect Edomae technique, peak-season fish, and rice seasoned with a kind of obsession you won't find anywhere else.

cards.name: Harutaka
cards.html:
01
Harutaka
Omakase Sushi · Ginza ↗ Map
Tokyo's only three-Michelin-starred sushi restaurant and the city's most celebrated counter. Chef Harutaka Takahashi — a Jiro Ono protégé — transforms the finest Edomae ingredients into 20-odd pieces of nigiri that feel simultaneously inevitable and surprising. Ten seats. Zero margin for error. One of the world's great meal experiences.

cards.name: Sushi Yoshitake
cards.html:
02
Sushi Yoshitake
Omakase Sushi · Ginza ↗ Map
Chef Masahiro Yoshitake's third-floor Ginza sanctum has held three Michelin stars for over a decade, and it remains one of the most accessible top-tier counters — accessible being relative. A new location offers slightly more seats and a rare private room, making it the go-to for groups seeking three-star omakase without the single-counter tension. The rice is exceptional. The aged fish, revelatory.

cards.name: Sushi Saito
cards.html:
03
Sushi Saito
Omakase Sushi · Roppongi Hills ↗ Map
The most mythologised reservation in Japan. Chef Takashi Saito's eight-seat counter operates on its own terms: no public booking, no walk-ins, and no amount of money alone will get you through the door. The sushi — bright, precise, deeply seasonal — is worth every hoop jumped. For guests with AmEx Platinum or Black, Pocket Concierge opens limited seats on the 1st of each month for two months out.

04
Sushi Kimura
Omakase Sushi · Futako-Tamagawa ↗ Map
One of Tokyo's most lauded two-star counters, Chef Saito Kimura's intimate room in Futako-Tamagawa rewards guests willing to venture outside central Tokyo. The Edomae technique is precise and thoughtful, with exceptional aged fish and perfectly tempered rice. One of the few omakase counters with an 18+ age policy. sections.title: Kaiseki
sections.desc: Japan's most refined cuisine, delivered across a dozen or more courses that follow the season with near-religious discipline. Every plate, every bowl, every vessel is chosen with the same care as what's inside it.

cards.name: Nihonryori RyuGin
cards.html:
01
Nihonryori RyuGin
Kaiseki · Hibiya ↗ Map
Chef Seiji Yamamoto holds three Michelin stars and a spot in the World's 100 Best Chefs top ten — a pairing that reflects the intellectual ambition of what happens at Ryugin. The cuisine is unmistakably kaiseki in its bones but arrives with a creative intensity that feels entirely its own. A sake pairing menu and a non-alcoholic tea pairing make this one of the most considered dining experiences in the city. Has held three stars since 2012.

cards.name: Ginza Fukuju
cards.html:
02
Ginza Fukuju
Kaiseki · Ginza ↗ Map
Chef Katsuhiro Onodera is a Fellow of the Japan Culinary Academy and one of the most influential figures in contemporary Japanese cuisine — a distinction earned through decades of disciplined cooking that never announces itself. His kaiseki moves between moments of delicate restraint and bold expressiveness; the tableware, selected to evoke each season, completes a visual and gastronomic experience of unusual depth. Two Michelin stars consistently since 2020.

03
Kutan
Kaiseki · Shintomi ↗ Map
Head Chef Kotaro Nakashima spent over 20 years training at renowned Japanese restaurants before opening Kutan in 2018, earning two Michelin stars within two years. The restaurant's striking white-and-red interior — a nod to the Japanese flag — creates an atmosphere as distinctive as the cooking. Only 13 seats ensures extraordinary focus and attention from the kitchen. A consistent favourite with discerning international guests.

sections.title: Ramen
sections.desc: Tokyo ramen is its own chapter of the story: shoyu-based, lighter than Sapporo or Fukuoka, and increasingly refined. Several of these shops held Michelin stars before the guide recategorised them; the quality hasn't changed.

cards.name: Ginza Hachio
cards.html:
01
Ginza Hachio
Ramen · Ginza ↗ Map
The most refined bowl of ramen in Tokyo — developed by a chef with 40 years in French cuisine who applied classical broth techniques to Japanese noodles. Duck, chicken and Rausu kelp create a soup of extraordinary depth without heaviness. Six counter seats, previously Michelin-starred (2022–23), now Bib Gourmand. The only ramen restaurant in Tokyo with a proper online reservation system — essential to secure, as walk-ins are rarely available.

cards.name: Nakiryu
cards.html:
02
Nakiryu
Ramen · Minami-Otsuka ↗ Map
Nakiryu held a Michelin star for six consecutive years (2017–2023) on the back of a tantanmen — the Japanese riff on Sichuan dandan noodles — so precisely constructed it became the reference point for the style. The spice, the sesame and the broth are balanced to a degree that's almost unsettling. Now a Bib Gourmand (2024–2026), the quality is unchanged; the ticketing system means a little patience earns a big reward.

cards.name: Sobahouse Konjiki Hototogisu
cards.html:
03
Sobahouse Konjiki Hototogisu
Ramen · Shinjuku ↗ Map
A former Michelin-starred shop (2022–23) that revamped its menu in 2024 toward bolder, more complex umami — a move that delighted regulars and puzzled nobody who'd eaten there before. The broth is a masterclass in layering. The noodles are perfect. This is ramen as serious cooking, presented in an unassuming shopfront that has been quietly excellent for nearly two decades. Arrive early for numbered tickets; the wait is worth it.

sections.title: Vegetarian & Vegan
sections.desc: From ancient Buddhist temple cuisine to avant-garde sustainable French, Tokyo's fully plant-based dining scene is more compelling than most cities manage with meat. These five restaurants need no apology for what they leave off the menu.

cards.name: Daigo
cards.html:
01
Daigo
Vegetarian & Vegan · Atago ↗ Map  Also in: Kaiseki
The flagship of this entire guide for vegetarians and vegans. Daigo's shojin ryori — the ancient Buddhist temple cuisine that is, in essence, Japan's original plant-based fine dining — has been practiced here since 1950. Fourth-generation Chef Yusuke Nomura prepares entirely vegan dishes (no meat, fish, eggs or dairy by design) with a precision and beauty that stuns guests who expect "vegetarian cuisine" to mean compromise. Michelin-starred since 2009, with a Green Star for sustainability since 2022. The finest all-plant meal you will eat in Asia, possibly anywhere. Also one of the few fine dining venues in this guide that accepts all ages, serves lunch, and is open almost every day of the year.

cards.name: NARISAWA
cards.html:
02
NARISAWA
Vegetarian & Vegan · Minami-Aoyama ↗ Map
Chef Yoshihiro Narisawa trained in the kitchens of Joël Robuchon and Paul Bocuse before returning to Japan to invent something entirely his own: "Innovative Satoyama Cuisine" — a genre drawn from Japan's forested landscape, fermentation traditions and sustainable farming. Two Michelin stars, a Michelin Green Star, and a decade in the World's 50 Best. The full dinner course of up to 14 dishes can be adapted entirely for vegetarians and vegans on request — not as a compromise, but as a parallel and equally ambitious expression of the same philosophy. At ¥89,500 (including a ¥8,000 booking fee via TABLEALL), this is Tokyo's definitive fine-dining answer to plant-based cooking at the highest level. Minimum two guests; advance notice required for dietary accommodation.
